name: Elisha
charge: Asking a double portion of the spirit; leaving the oxen and following, and refusing Naaman's reward
summary: Called from ploughing, Elisha fed the people and followed Elijah. He asked a double portion of his spirit and continued the ministry after his master was taken. He supplied households, restored the Shunammite’s son, refused Naaman’s reward, and fed the Syrians delivered into Samaria. After his death, a man revived upon touching his bones.
offense: Elisha was ploughing when Elijah cast his mantle upon him. He left the oxen, asked to kiss his father and mother, and returned to prepare a farewell meal. He slew a yoke of oxen, boiled the flesh with their instruments, fed the people, and arose to minister to Elijah (1 Kings 19:19-21). The call was answered by a change of service, not merely an expression of admiration for the prophet. When Elijah's departure approached, Elisha would not leave him at Gilgal, Bethel, or Jericho. He crossed Jordan with him and asked for a double portion of his spirit. Elijah called it a hard thing and gave the condition that Elisha see him taken (2 Kings 2:1-10). The request concerned the power required to continue the work, not wealth or a place at the king's table. After Naaman's cleansing, Elisha refused the gift pressed upon him, swearing by the Lord before whom he stood that he would receive none (2 Kings 5:15-16). Gehazi afterward pursued what his master refused. The same opportunity distinguished service from covetousness. The healing was not to be turned into a private bargain by a servant who had not supplied its power. At Dothan, surrounded by the Syrian host, Elisha answered his servant's fear by praying that his eyes be opened. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15-17). Elisha did not deny the surrounding army; he knew it was not the only host present. He sought that his servant see the protection already there.
judgment: Elisha saw Elijah taken and received the mantle that fell. Returning to Jordan, he struck the water and called upon the Lord God of Elijah. The waters divided, and the sons of the prophets recognised that Elijah's spirit rested upon him (2 Kings 2:11-15). The departed master was not the source exhausted by his departure. The Lord remained with the servant appointed to continue. His ministry supplied households and preserved life: the widow's oil paid her debt, the Shunammite received her son alive, harmful pottage was made safe, and a hundred men ate from twenty barley loaves and left food remaining (2 Kings 4:1-7, 32-44). The wonders were not detached displays. They answered debt, bereavement, hunger, and danger among the people. When the Syrians sent to seize him were led into Samaria, the king asked whether to kill them. Elisha commanded that food and water be set before them and that they return to their master. They ate and departed (2 Kings 6:18-23). Power to deliver an enemy into the city did not require that power to be used for slaughter. The prophet who announced judgments also directed mercy where the Lord had given that charge. Elisha eventually became sick and died, but the Lord's power was not buried with him. A dead man cast into his sepulchre touched his bones, revived, and stood upon his feet (2 Kings 13:20-21). Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 48:12-14 remembers both the wonders of his life and the marvel after his death. His strength had never resided in possessions gathered from those he helped, but in the Lord whose word he served.
